question: What is the main difference between a standard IV infusion and a blood transfusion?

options.A: Transfusions never require a special intravenous line
options.B: Infusions are always given faster than blood transfusions
options.C: Infusions can only use blood products while transfusions use plain water
options.D: Infusions deliver fluids or medications while transfusions replace blood components

explanation: You've got this! Regular IV fluids give water, salts, or drugs, while blood transfusions specifically replace parts of the blood like red cells or plasma. Simple and clear! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to be extra careful when giving IV fluids or blood products?

options.A: Patients always feel severe pain when any fluid enters a vein
options.B: Every procedure carries inherent risks such as fluid overload or severe reactions
options.C: Intravenous lines are guaranteed to clog within one hour
options.D: Hospital management requires extra paperwork for all fluid bags

explanation: Even though giving fluids is an everyday task, putting anything straight into the bloodstream can cause rapid changes or reactions. Staying alert keeps our patients safe! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h1)

question: What is the main feature of crystalloid IV solutions like normal saline?

options.A: They consist of massive protein structures that stay trapped in blood vessels
options.B: They can only be administered through central venous catheters
options.C: They are harvested directly from human blood donors
options.D: They contain small molecules that easily cross membranes into body tissues

explanation: Think of crystalloids as small-molecule solutions that easily move out of the blood vessels and into the tissues. Great concept to keep in mind for your ward postings! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h2)

question: Which blood product is best to give a patient who is bleeding heavily because they lack clotting factors?
explanation: Fresh Frozen Plasma is packed with the vital clotting factors needed to help stop bleeding. You're building great clinical judgment! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h2)

question: Which IV solution is the ONLY safe one to hang alongside a blood transfusion?
explanation: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) plays nice with blood! Other fluids like dextrose can cause red blood cells to burst (hemolysis), while Ringer's has calcium that can cause clotting in the tubing. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h3)

question: Why is a bedside double-check with two nurses a must before starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: To make sure the nurse finishes the shift on time
options.B: To prevent fatal errors by confirming exact patient and blood product matching
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the blood bag before hanging
options.D: To ensure the blood pump is plugged into a backup generator

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are better than one! Checking details together ensures the right blood goes to the right patient every single time. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h3)

question: How long should a nurse stay right by the patient's side after a blood transfusion starts?

options.A: Only until the pump is turned on
options.C: Until the entire bag is empty

explanation: Most serious transfusion reactions happen fast at the very beginning. Staying close for those first 15 minutes lets you catch and treat any reaction early! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h4)

question: What is the main reason a bag of blood must be completely infused within four hours?

options.A: To ensure the infusion pump battery does not run out of power
options.B: To prevent dangerous bacterial growth in the blood at room temperature
options.C: To stop the patient from becoming too cold during the procedure
options.D: To prevent the red blood cells from settling at the bottom of the bag

explanation: Blood is warm and rich in nutrients—bacteria love it too! Finishing it within four hours stops germs from multiplying in the bag. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h4)

question: What is the VERY FIRST thing a nurse must do if a patient shows signs of a transfusion reaction?

options.C: Slow down the infusion pump rate

explanation: Safety first! Stopping the flow immediately keeps any more of the incompatible blood from entering their body. You're thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h5)

question: A patient having a blood transfusion suddenly develops fever, chills, and sharp lower back pain. What is likely happening?
explanation: Lower back pain, fever, and chills are classic warning signs that the body is reacting against the red blood cells. Great clinical cue to remember! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h5)
